In the aperiodic mode the SG (synchronization gap) timer and the TG (terminal gap) timer are very important. The TI does not effect the operation of the data transfer in the aperiodic mode.

The next smallest TG is the third system, which transmits its data and resets its SG. Remember, the SG has to fully elapse before the TG timer will start, and the SG resets when the bus is active until it has had a chance to fully elapse.

After the SG timer has fully elapsed, the TG (terminal gap) timer begins. Every system has their own value for the TG timer. Think of this value as a ticket number. The bus will allow each of the systems to transmit once in the order of their ticket numbers.

The SG (synchronization gap) timer does not effect the operation of data transfer in the periodic mode, however, it is still active in the system. The SG timer for a system is reset when its data has been sent. The SG timer after being reset will start when there is nothing happening on the bus.
Remember, the SG and TG timers are very important in the aperiodic mode but, in the periodic mode the TI is the most important timer.

The best way to understand the process of data transfer is to use a simple analogy. Let's say that the subsystem is a person, the common memory is a mailbox, the terminal controller is the post office, and the rest is the mail transportation system.

Data is encoded into Manchester as it leaves the terminal controller chip. Data received by the terminal controller is decoded from Manchester and then sent to other parts of the chip. Remember, all data on the global side of the terminal controller is modulated, all data inside and on the local side is not modulated.

Now that the post office (terminal controller) has accepted the package (data), it will process the package (data) and deliver it to someone's mailbox (common memory). Once the package (data) has been delivered, someone (subsystem) can check the mailbox (common memory) to see if their package arrived.

All data to and from the Serial Interface Module (SIM) and the terminal controller is encoded using Manchester code. Manchester code is a modulation technique that allows easy generation of the original clock. In other words, something receiving the data can determine the clock speed of the sender by analyzing the signal.
Below is an example of how data is encoded using this technique. Notice that a high is represented by a high to low sequence, and a low is represented by a low to high sequence.

The post office (terminal controller) receives a package (data) from the mail transportation system (bus). The post office (terminal controller) then looks at the label of the package (data). If the post office (terminal controller) finds that the label corresponds to someone in this district (PROM) then it will accept the package (data).

DEFINITION

INDUCED - Inducing a signal is transferring a signal from one line to another by magnetic induction. By applying a changing voltage to the coil of a transformer, a magnetic field is created that induces current into the bus wires. This induced current can then be induced back into the coil of a transformer.
